sourceTitle: A Night at the Space Club
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: EN/A2 independently drafted Asteroids Reading test; not reviewed by second teacher.

tabs.title: Understanding the message
tabs.description: Interpret the passage and its purpose.

tabs.title: Reasons and connections
tabs.description: Find explanations supported by the text.

tabs.title: Use what you have read
tabs.description: Apply the information to new situations.

questions.q: What surprises many people about the asteroid belt?
choices: It has no asteroids at all.
There is a lot of empty space between its objects.
It is a road that astronauts can drive on.
It is found much closer to Earth than the Moon.
questions.explanation: The teacher points out that the belt is not crowded because the rocks are far apart.

questions.q: Why does the club teacher say that a near-Earth asteroid is not automatically dangerous?
choices: Scientists cannot calculate its path.
Space rocks near Earth are always tiny.
The Moon keeps every asteroid away.
Passing near Earth and colliding with it are different events.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly distinguishes an object coming near Earth from one actually hitting it.

questions.q: What do the students discover when the telescope does not show an asteroid?
choices: Their teacher has forgotten to prepare the telescope.
The club has to meet during the daytime instead.
They can still study marks made by space rocks on the Moon.
The Moon is too far away to see clearly.
questions.explanation: The students observe lunar craters even though the asteroids themselves are too faint.

questions.q: What does Nina understand after watching the DART film?
choices: A small planned push may change how a space object moves.
All asteroids now follow a new path around Earth.
The school telescope is strong enough to move space rocks.
Scientists have stopped looking for dangerous asteroids.
questions.explanation: The film shows that a spacecraft can give a small asteroid moon a push and change its orbit.

questions.q: Why do scientists keep observing a newly found asteroid?
choices: They want to make it easier to photograph the Moon.
New observations help them predict its future path more accurately.
Most asteroids change their size every day.
The first observations show exactly where it will go.
questions.explanation: More observations reduce uncertainty about a newly discovered object's orbit.

questions.q: Why are old craters easier to see on the Moon than on Earth?
choices: They were made by larger rocks on the Moon.
Earth has no old craters at all.
The Moon lacks wind and rain that would slowly hide them.
The Moon is closer to most asteroids than Earth.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the Moon's lack of weather with Earth's erosion.

questions.q: Why was the DART collision useful for scientists?
choices: It showed that telescopes cannot find asteroids.
It protected Earth from a collision that was already happening.
It destroyed the asteroid belt.
It tested whether a spacecraft could change an asteroid moon's orbit.
questions.explanation: DART intentionally struck Dimorphos and its orbital period changed, proving a method could be tested.

questions.q: A new object is spotted near Earth, but there are few observations. What is a sensible next step?
choices: Warn everyone that a collision is certain.
Take more measurements before drawing strong conclusions.
Stop using computers to calculate orbits.
Assume it will move away without any further checks.
questions.explanation: The teacher describes repeated observations as necessary for a reliable orbit prediction.

questions.q: A pupil wants to explain how craters form but cannot photograph an asteroid. What could they do?
choices: Use a picture of the Moon's craters as supporting evidence.
Say that craters disappear immediately in space.
Explain that the Moon's craters were made by rain.
Claim that a school telescope can see all small asteroids.
questions.explanation: The club uses visible lunar craters to discuss the long-term effects of impacts.

questions.q: Which conclusion best combines the last two parts of Nina's club visit?
choices: Watching the Moon means we no longer need spacecraft.
Space travel has made asteroids completely harmless.
Photographs of craters are not useful for science.
Observation and experiments can both help us prepare for space hazards.
questions.explanation: Nina experiences observation through the telescope and learning about a controlled spacecraft experiment.
